Question: What does it mean when a Google interviewer says, “There is no feedback on this one” after an interview question?
Old_Answer: After an interview, interviewers are required to give detailed feedback according to several criteria. However, over all the time that the interviewer and candidate interact, there are periods when candidates are not judged, roughly the first 5 minutes and the last 5. It can be difficult to detect when the interview time proper actually starts, versus when the interviewer is still trying to build rapport. Likewise, candidates can feel that they are being evaluated as they ask questions, and feel forced to pick questions as a last opportunity to score points versus as a chance to get a candid answer on something they want to know. So, some interviewers like to signal when the candidate is “off the hook”. If a candidate says or does something completely outrageous during that time, the interviewer will still have to report it, but the bar for outrageous is pretty high, like: personal attacks.
Answer_with_writing_sample: When a Google interviewer says, “There is no feedback on this one,” it can feel a bit like a foggy day in San Francisco – you know the sun is shining somewhere, but it’s hard to see it clearly. This phrase typically means that they can't provide specific insights on your performance for that particular question, which can be frustrating for candidates who are seeking constructive criticism to improve. It might stem from a variety of reasons – perhaps the interviewer is bound by company policy or they simply believe the assessment is inherently subjective. In any case, it's important not to take it personally; remember, interviews are as much about fit as they are about skills. Instead of dwelling on the lack of feedback, focus on the broader picture and approach the interview as a learning experience, honing in on what you can control: your preparation and mindset for the next opportunity.
Answer_with_user_profile: When a Google interviewer says, “There is no feedback on this one” after an interview question, it typically indicates a few key aspects of their interviewing process. Firstly, it suggests that the question was intended to assess your thought process rather than yield a definitive right or wrong answer. Interviewers at Google often value an applicant's problem-solving approach, creativity, and analytical skills more than simply arriving at a correct solution. Therefore, if no feedback is provided, it may mean that they were looking for insight into how you approach challenges, rather than a specific answer. Secondly, it might imply that the question posed was subjective or open-ended, making it difficult for the interviewer to provide constructive criticism or affirmation. Lastly, this phrase may reflect the interviewer's style; some prefer to let candidates work through questions without immediate guidance, allowing them to showcase their independent thinking. In Google’s competitive interview environment, it’s important to remain calm and focused, even when faced with non-specific feedback. Remember, the goal is to demonstrate your reasoning, thought processes, and how you handle ambiguity—qualities that can resonate with the interviewers and play a vital role in assessing your fit for the company. Don't be disheartened; rather, view it as an opportunity to shine in your logical reasoning and ability to navigate complex problems without relying on immediate feedback.
Answer_with_full_information: When a Google interviewer says, “There is no feedback on this one,” it can feel a little disconcerting, but it’s essential to understand its implications in the context of the interview process. This phrase typically indicates that the interviewer is likely not looking for you to dig deeper into your answer or request clarification. Instead, they might be signaling that your response didn't necessarily align with the expected answer, but they don't want to delve into specifics. It can also mean that they don’t want to bias your responses for the remaining questions—keeping the evaluation consistent and fair. In the tech giant's rigorous interview environment, responses are often evaluated against a set of criteria, and not every answer receives a detailed critique. So, when faced with this kind of remark, instead of dwelling on it, see it as an opportunity to move forward without second-guessing yourself. Use this moment to refocus your energy on the next question rather than concerning yourself with what could have gone wrong. Remember, interviews are not just about getting every answer right; they're about demonstrating your thought process, problem-solving skills, and how you handle challenges. Thus, staying resilient and adaptive in these trying moments can not only lighten the atmosphere but also showcase your ability to navigate uncertainty—an asset in any role at Google or beyond.

Question: Do big tech companies like Google, Apple, Microsoft, etc. care about what university you go to?
Old_Answer: yes and no. If you’re an experienced hire, then where you got your degree from and whether you have a degree to begin with has close to 0 impact. However, as of 2024 my impression is that it’s very difficult to get an entry-level technical position outside of campus recruiting programs, internships etc., which are targeting some specific universities. This wasn’t true a few years ago (ie pre-pandemic) at a time when a self-taught person could get an interview for an entry-level position. Now that self-taught candidate is pretty much expected to acquire experience elsewhere and reach the point where they can apply to slightly more senior jobs.
Answer_with_writing_sample: While there’s no one-size-fits-all answer, it's fair to say that big tech companies like Google, Apple, and Microsoft do take your educational background into account, but it’s not the be-all and end-all. Having a degree from a prestigious university can certainly give you a leg up, as it often indicates a certain level of rigor and competence in your field. However, I’ve seen plenty of candidates from lesser-known institutions who have outshone Ivy League grads simply because they had the right skills and experience. In the end, what really matters is your ability to demonstrate your knowledge through projects, internships, and interviews. If you’ve got a solid portfolio and can prove that you can tackle real-world problems, you might find that your university doesn’t matter as much as you think. So, focus on building your skills and showcasing your work—those will speak volumes when you step into that interview room.
Answer_with_user_profile: Big tech companies like Google, Apple, and Microsoft increasingly emphasize skills and experience over the specific university a candidate attended. While prestigious institutions can provide networking opportunities and foundational knowledge, these companies are more focused on a candidate's ability to innovate and adapt in a fast-paced tech environment. Many tech giants have implemented alternative hiring practices, such as skills assessments and coding challenges, which help them identify talent regardless of educational background. Furthermore, some companies have broadened their recruitment efforts by actively seeking candidates from diverse educational paths, including coding boot camps and online courses, recognizing that talent can be found outside traditional universities. That said, attending a well-regarded university may enhance a candidate's initial visibility and credibility, but it is no longer the sole determinant of career success in the tech industry. Demonstrating hands-on experience, relevant projects, and soft skills often outweighs the name on a diploma. Hence, while a prestigious university can provide some advantages, it is ultimately a candidate's skills, passion, and cultural fit that truly matter in securing a position at these companies.
Answer_with_full_information: When it comes to big tech companies like Google, Apple, and Microsoft, the emphasis placed on the university you attended is nuanced and multifaceted. While it's undeniable that they initially consider educational backgrounds during the hiring process, particularly for entry-level positions, this is far from the sole determining factor. These companies are increasingly focused on the skills, experiences, and innovative thinking that candidates bring to the table. With the rise of coding bootcamps, online courses, and self-directed learning, many hiring managers now value practical expertise and demonstrated problem-solving abilities over prestigious degree titles. Internships, side projects, and contributions to open-source communities can often carry as much weight—if not more—than the name of your alma mater. Moreover, tech giants are waking up to the need for a diverse talent pool that reflects a variety of perspectives, which has led them to broaden their recruitment strategies. They want individuals who are not only technically proficient but also possess the soft skills necessary for collaboration and creativity in a fast-paced environment. Ultimately, it’s about what you can do rather than where you learned to do it. For aspiring candidates, networking, continuous learning, and staying abreast of industry trends will likely prove more beneficial in gaining traction with these companies than any specific university affiliation.

Question: How difficult is it for senior software engineers to get an interview at Google?
Old_Answer: Google’s “senior software engineer” / L5 is probably in the upper range of what’s understood by “senior software engineer” in terms of work experience. It is quite an achievement to be promoted to that level, and that’s something that happens usually between 5 to 8 years after being hired. By the way, there are people who elect to never go for that level and stay 15 years at L4. There are a lot of places in tech where you can become “senior software engineer” after 2 or 3 years of experience. It’s really up to any organization to determine where to draw the line between junior and senior and what level of experience represents the pivot. The TL;DR is that in order to be invited to interview as a senior engineer, a candidate must have experience comparable to what a “homegrown” senior engineer at Google would have.

So, while getting an interview may not be as tough as it is for entry-level candidates, the challenge really lies in how well you can perform when the spotlight is on you. It’s always beneficial to put some time into honing your interview skills, even if you think you know your stuff; consider it your warm-up before you jump into anything competitive. Remember, interviews are as much about how you approach problems as they are about solving them, so gear up accordingly!

Question: How do you interview for software engineering positions when the candidate has no prior experience in the field?
Old_Answer: How would I interview a candidate who has no industry experience, exactly like a candidate who does. They would get the same coding tests and the same behavioral interviews. A lot of the professional experience of a candidate can be used for these behavioral interviews regardless of their actual role. How would I prepare as a candidate had I no experience as a software engineer, well, how I’ve done it when I interviewed as a software engineer from another career. I prepared for the coding test until I felt I was ready. There’s ample material available, much more than when I made that career change. Candidates won’t get a pass just because they had a different job title before, but they also get a shot at it even though they don’t necessarily come from a software engineering background.
Answer_with_writing_sample: When interviewing candidates with no prior experience in software engineering, it’s crucial to shift your focus from technical skills to their problem-solving abilities and willingness to learn. You want to look for candidates who demonstrate a passion for technology, even if they haven’t had formal experience. Ask them about personal projects, coding boot camps, or even how they’ve taught themselves new programming languages. Assess their fundamental understanding of concepts rather than coding fluency by presenting hypothetical scenarios or conceptual questions. In my experience, a candidate's thought process in tackling a problem often speaks louder than their past work history. Remember, everyone starts somewhere, and someone who shows enthusiasm and a growth mindset can often outperform a well-experienced candidate who is set in their ways. It’s about finding that potential and nurturing it; after all, every seasoned engineer was once a beginner.
Answer_with_user_profile: When interviewing candidates for software engineering positions without prior experience in the field, it's crucial to focus on their foundational skills, problem-solving abilities, and aptitude for learning rather than their direct work history. Start by assessing their understanding of basic programming concepts through questions or coding tests that reveal their logical reasoning and ability to apply what they've learned, even if informally or in personal projects. It's also important to gauge their familiarity with relevant tools or languages they may have studied, perhaps through coursework or self-directed learning. Incorporate behavioral questions to evaluate their resilience, teamwork, and communication skills—qualities that are vital in a collaborative engineering environment. Ask situational questions that help uncover how they approach challenges, demonstrating their critical thinking and adaptability. In addition, explore their passion for technology by discussing personal projects, coding bootcamps, or relevant online courses they’ve undertaken. Finally, introduce a culture fit assessment, since someone with great enthusiasm for the field can often prove to be more valuable than an equally skilled candidate with experience but lacking motivation. Overall, convey an understanding that many successful engineers have forged their paths through unconventional routes and emphasize the importance of a growth mindset and willingness to learn in your evaluation process.
Answer_with_full_information: Interviewing for software engineering positions when the candidate has no prior experience can be both challenging and rewarding. First and foremost, it's essential to focus on the candidate's problem-solving abilities and potential for growth rather than their experience. Start with a discussion around their educational background—any relevant coursework, projects they've completed, or any self-driven learning initiatives like online courses or personal coding projects. Additionally, gauge their enthusiasm for the field: a genuine passion for technology and software development can often translate into a strong work ethic and willingness to learn. Lastly, remember to create a supportive environment during the interview. Question: How should an interview with a software developer be concluded if it is clear that the candidate will not be hired?
Old_Answer: Let’s step out of the interview room a little bit. Candidate Alice interviews for BigTech co. The next day, she meets Bob for coffee. How are you, asks Bob. Well, I interviewed for BigTech co yesterday, says Alice. So, how was it? wonders Bob. The interview experience is designed, so that we can influence what Alice will say next. “Oh, they were really super nice, but I don’t think I am going to pass. Too bad, because it looked really cool. “ Or “I don’t care, they’re pompous assholes, I won’t take an offer no matter with how many 0s. “ Candidates talk far and wide about their interviewing experience, so a positive or negative experience can have a profound impact on the employer brand. This should inform how to talk to candidates, regardless of their performance.
Answer_with_writing_sample: Concluding an interview with a candidate who clearly isn't a fit can be a delicate situation, but it’s crucial to handle it with transparency and professionalism. Ideally, you should provide some constructive feedback; it signals respect for the candidate's effort and time, and can help them improve. A simple acknowledgment of their skills is nice, but also gently hinting at areas where they can focus on development—be it technical skills, problem-solving approaches, or even communication—can be invaluable for their growth. It’s also good to express appreciation for their interest in the role and the company—they’ve taken the time to prepare, and that should be recognized. Finally, wishing them luck in their job search leaves the door open for future interactions and conveys that you value every person who crosses your path, even if they’re not the right fit at this moment. It’s all about creating a positive experience, ensuring that, even in rejection, dignity is maintained.
Answer_with_user_profile: Concluding an interview with a software developer, or any candidate for that matter, requires a blend of professionalism, empathy, and clarity, especially if it’s clear that they will not be hired. Begin by thanking the candidate for their time and effort in coming to the interview. Acknowledge their skills and any positive attributes observed during the conversation. It's essential to be honest yet tactful; you might say something like, “While we appreciate your enthusiasm and certain skills you demonstrated, we have determined that we are looking for a slightly different fit for this position.” Avoid delving too deeply into specific reasons unless the candidate seeks feedback, and be prepared to provide constructive insights if they request it. This shows you care about their development and respects their interest in your company. Offer encouragement for their job search and perhaps suggest they continue honing specific skills or experiences that align better with industry needs. Lastly, inform them to expect a formal follow-up notification regarding the outcome, reiterating your appreciation and wishing them success in their future endeavors. This approach not only maintains the candidate's dignity but also helps to foster a positive reputation for your company in the competitive job market.
Answer_with_full_information: Concluding an interview with a software developer who clearly isn’t the right fit is crucial, not just for the candidate’s experience but also for maintaining the company’s reputation. Start by expressing gratitude for their time and effort in preparing for the interview. It’s important to create a respectful atmosphere. You might say something like, “Thank you for taking the time to meet with us today. We appreciate your interest in our team.” Then, provide some constructive feedback if possible, focusing on specific areas of improvement that could benefit their future applications. For example, you might mention they could enhance their coding skills in a particular area or work on articulating their thoughts during technical discussions. After delivering this feedback, you can gently inform them that you won’t be moving forward with their application. Be tactful; you might say, “While we enjoyed speaking with you, we’ve decided to move forward with other candidates for this role.” Finally, end on a positive note; encourage them to apply for other positions in the future if it feels appropriate and offer your best wishes for their job search. It’s essential to ensure that the candidate leaves feeling like they gained something from the experience, rather than just a rejection. By doing this, you're helping to foster a positive experience that they can communicate to others, reflecting well on your organization even when the outcome isn’t what they hoped for.

Question: What is the process for someone with no college education to work as a software engineer at Google or Facebook? How long does this take?
Old_Answer: Education gives a leg up for candidates because Google and Meta are actively recruiting in certain campuses. The easiest way is to get an internship and convert it into an offer. But in the general case, you get hired by passing an interview, which takes 2 steps: being invited to interview, and performing well at the interview. Anyone can succeed in step 2 regardless of education as long as they have the skills, and anyone who has the disposition can learn the skills. When you don’t have a degree, it is step 1 which is harder. When I was working at Facebook, I had 2 teammates that didn’t have a college degree. Prior to Facebook, one was a key contributor to an influential open source library, and the other had already a resume more impressive than most people twice his age, having started a sold a business. In my personal case, I had a degree, just not in computer science. But what I had was a well-read blog. This helped enter the hiring pipeline.

First, focus on building a solid foundation in programming languages like Python, Java, or JavaScript—there are plenty of free resources out there, from online courses to coding boot camps that can help you. Start working on personal projects and contributing to open source to build a portfolio that demonstrates your skills—this is crucial because it will serve as your proof of competence when you don’t have a degree to fall back on. Networking is also key; attend tech meetups, hackathons, or join online communities where you can connect with other developers and potentially find mentors or referrals. In terms of time, the journey can vary—some people might secure a position at a major company within a year or two if they’re really dedicated, while others might take longer to gain the necessary experience and confidence. Ultimately, it’s about commitment, continuous learning, and showcasing your abilities over traditional qualifications. Remember, many successful engineers have carved their path with tenacity and creativity, so stay persistent and adaptable!

Question: Why does Google show Quora answers when you search a question, as if those hold any validity? So many people dont realize how incorrect most answers are. Am I the only one who thinks they should be excluded?
Old_Answer: As someone who has spent a lot of time using Quora and understanding Google Search, I believe I can give a decent answer to this question. When you think of search engines of the 90s, you have that search box where a user is going to enter text, and then after they submit the search, they are going to get a series of links that contain the text searched. This is not how modern search engines work (Google or otherwise). Today, what people enter in the search box is less a phrase to look for in a vast pile of documents, and more a command. Users expect to get something relevant in response to that command. Technically, what people put in the search box is called a query. The first thing the search engine is going to do, “understanding”, is to extract an intent from the query. An intent is a formal representation of what the user wants. To take the quintessential example of Google if a user types “obama height” they do not want to find all the documents that contain the phrase obama height, but most likely want to know how tall Barack Obama is. Extracting an intent is not enough. There are hundreds of servlets which are treating a query and which are either detecting an intent in a query or assigning metadata to the query, such as: how polite is the tone, as this yields different results. So typically, many intents are extracted. Next the search engine is going to rank these intents. Sometimes one intent is overwhelmingly likely, and it’s very unlikely that the user actually meant something else. Sometimes, it’s not as clear cut. So in our example, maybe the user wanted the height of Michelle Obama. Maybe by some logic they wanted to know Trump’s or Biden’s. And maybe, you know what, they wanted to see webpages that talk about “height” and “obama”. OK, so now Google has several intents ranked. What to do next is fulfillment and execution. Fulfillment means that it’s going to prepare answers corresponding to all the intents. Execution means it’s going to actually get those answers from the servers and render them on screen, and is not super relevant for this question. In the case of “obama height”, in google’s parliance there are a couple of intents which are going to be fulfilled, one is “knowledge base lookup” and one is “web search”. Knowledge base lookup means that the user is looking for a well-known facet (“height”) of an well-known entity (“former US president Barack Obama”) is Google’s representation of the world, its knowledge base. BTW the answer is 6′2″, a fact which is drilled into the mind of anyone who works or has worked in Google Search. When there is a “hit” for knowledge base, or really for any of the intents it understands, then Google is going to answer to the intent with a special card. That’s the happy path because if Google actually guessed the intent of the user, then the special card is going to do a much better job at responding to it than expecting them to click on one of 10 blue links. But web search is almost always fired as well, which is the list of blue links with a blurb. So on to Quora content. Quora is used by Google’s knowledge base as one of many trusted sources of information. This doesn’t mean that Google feels that whatever is in a Quora answer is absolute truth. But there is some curation, there is some validation by other users through upvotes and downvotes, so it’s much better than an arbitrary piece of web content. That is not foolproof. A notorious example is when some folks decided to update the height of cartoon character Caillou on the Fandom wiki (another trusted source, due to its human curation). Caillou, a toddler, still comes up as being 5′11″ if you google “caillou height”. Google is well aware that “it happens” and generally doesn’t care as long as directionally, content from trusted sources is more reliable on average. It also has mechanisms to address poor results. As a user you can report an answer as poor (and as a human you can also try to tweak the source of the knowledge base which I suspect is still going on with Caillou). So the answer of your question is that for the queries for which there are Quora answer, Google doesn’t have more authoritative content and it believes it is more useful to the user than just sending them to a list of links. Google also found that more often than not, when displayed, Quora content is actually helpful.

Question: What is the reason for the high number of failures in technical interviews at Google and Facebook? Is it due to lack of preparation from candidates, or is there another reason?
Old_Answer: Google gets about 3 million applications per year. There are very few open positions. That’s all you need to know. During a big part of the 2010s, the reasoning behind tech hiring is that someone who is good enough should get a job. This may still be true in some companies that are in very fast growth. In most of the tech world though, candidates are applying for a specific role in a specific team, so there will be a limited number of candidates who will get an offer. This allows employers to move the bar up. So sure, there is a lot of advice out there for candidates, and a lot of it makes sense. But there is no such thing as “the most common mistake” which if addressed will guarantee a spot. At the end of the day, interviews are complex human interactions with a lot of variables in play, evaluations are subjective to some extent, hiring committee is also composed of humans and there are lots of factors that contribute to a decision.
Answer_with_writing_sample: The high number of failures in technical interviews at Google and Facebook can be attributed to several factors, but lack of preparation is a major player in that game. Many candidates walk in with the belief that their experience or background alone will suffice, and that’s a quick ticket to disappointment. The interviews are designed to test not only your knowledge but your problem-solving approach and coding skills under pressure – it’s a whole different beast compared to the day-to-day work. Those who treat it like just another conversation often find themselves blindsided. Furthermore, the sheer competitive atmosphere means that many candidates are up against a well-prepared pool, and if you’re just winging it, you’ll likely flop. Another reason could be the misalignment of expectations; candidates sometimes don’t fully understand the role and the specific skills needed, leading to a mismatch in what they showcase versus what the interviewers are looking for. So, while a lack of preparation is significant, it’s also about not genuinely grasping the challenge laid out before you.

Ultimately, while thorough preparation is crucial, it is equally important for candidates to understand the interview dynamics, think critically, communicate effectively, and remain adaptable throughout the process. Thus, preparation must encompass not only technical skills but also a strategic approach to the interview experience itself.
